title: Virtual Memory
tagline: How every program believes it owns the whole machine

sections.content:
Open a terminal, type `top`, and count the processes: dozens, sometimes hundreds of programs are all running simultaneously on the same physical machine. Each of those programs contains code that accesses memory by referring to addresses — specific numbered locations in RAM. But here is the puzzle: two different programs might both try to use address `0x401000`, and yet they never collide. They see completely different data at the same address. How is that possible?

The answer is **virtual memory** — one of the most elegant abstractions in all of computer science. Every running process lives inside a private illusion: it believes it has exclusive access to a vast, contiguous block of memory that starts at address zero and extends for terabytes. This illusion is maintained jointly by the **operating system** and a hardware unit inside the CPU called the **Memory Management Unit (MMU)**. Every address a process names is a *virtual* address; the MMU silently translates it to a *physical* address in actual RAM before the memory access occurs — typically in nanoseconds, invisibly to the running program.

Virtual memory solves four critical problems at once. **Isolation**: if process A writes to address `0x1000`, it cannot corrupt process B's data at the same virtual address, because both map to different physical locations. **Simplicity**: the linker and compiler can assume a clean, uniform address space for every program regardless of what else happens to be loaded in RAM. **Overcommit**: programs can reserve more virtual address space than physical RAM actually exists; physical pages are allocated lazily on first access. **Sharing**: multiple processes can map the same physical page read-only (e.g., the C standard library loaded once in RAM but visible in every process's address space).

This chapter builds the complete mental model: how physical RAM is divided into pages and frames, how the OS builds a page table to record the mapping, how the MMU and TLB accelerate every lookup, what happens during a page fault, how swap space extends apparent RAM, how multi-level page tables tame 64-bit address spaces, and what all of this means for the software you write.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P1["Process 1\naddr 0x1000"] --> MMU["MMU\n+ TLB"]
  P2["Process 2\naddr 0x1000"] --> MMU
  MMU --> F1["Physical Frame\n0x3A000 (RAM)"]
  MMU --> F2["Physical Frame\n0x8C000 (RAM)"]
  MMU --> SW["Swap on Disk"]
sections.caption: Two processes reference the same virtual address 0x1000, but the MMU translates each to a different physical frame — or fetches a page from disk on demand.

sections.title: The Hotel Front Desk
sections.content:
Picture a hotel where every guest is handed a key labelled 'Room 1' through 'Room N'. Each guest genuinely believes they have their own private Room 1. But the front desk keeps a secret ledger: Guest A's Room 1 is actually physical room 201; Guest B's Room 1 is physical room 547. They never collide because the desk intercepts every room request and consults the ledger before pointing guests anywhere.

If a guest asks for a room that is temporarily being redecorated and is not available right now (its contents are stored offsite), the desk pauses the guest, sends a porter to retrieve the room's contents, and only then lets the guest in. That retrieval delay corresponds to a **page fault** — the OS fetching a memory page from disk.

The front-desk clerk also maintains a personal pocket notebook of the most recently looked-up room assignments so they don't have to search the full ledger every time. This notebook is the **TLB** (Translation Lookaside Buffer) — a tiny, blazing-fast hardware cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations. A hit in the notebook resolves the request instantly; a miss means consulting the full ledger (the page table) in RAM.

sections.title: Pages and Frames: The Unit of Memory Management
sections.content:
Virtual memory does not manage individual bytes — that would require an impossibly large lookup table. Instead, both virtual and physical address spaces are divided into fixed-size chunks:

- A **page** is a contiguous block of virtual address space, typically **4 KB** (4096 bytes) on x86 and ARM. The OS can also use **huge pages** of 2 MB or 1 GB for workloads with large, contiguous allocations (databases, HPC).
- A **frame** (or **page frame**) is the corresponding 4 KB block of physical RAM.

Pages and frames are always the same size — that is the key. It means you can slot any virtual page into any physical frame, regardless of where they sit numerically. The OS tracks which frames are free with a **frame allocator** (often a bitmap or free list).

Because the page size is a power of two, an address splits cleanly into two fields: the upper bits identify which page (or frame), and the lower bits are the **byte offset** within that page. For 4 KB pages the lower 12 bits are the offset (since 2¹² = 4096), and the upper bits are the page number.

The split is important in hardware: the page number must be translated by the MMU, but the offset passes through unchanged, because once you find the correct physical frame, the byte's position within it is the same as its position within the virtual page.

This design means the OS only needs to record one translation entry per page, not one per byte. For a 4 GB address space with 4 KB pages there are only about one million entries to manage — feasible. For a 64-bit address space the number of *possible* pages is astronomical, which is why multi-level page tables are necessary (covered below).

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  VA["Virtual Address\n(48 bits)"] --> PN["Page Number\n(upper 36 bits)"]
  VA --> OFF["Byte Offset\n(lower 12 bits)"]
  PN --> PT["Page Table\nLookup"]
  PT --> FN["Frame Number"]
  FN --> PA["Physical Address"]
  OFF --> PA
sections.caption: A virtual address splits into page number (looked up in the page table) and byte offset (passed through unchanged). Combining the frame number with the offset gives the physical address.

sections.title: The Page Table: The OS Ledger
sections.content:
Every process has its own **page table** — a data structure, usually stored in RAM, that records the virtual-page-to-physical-frame mapping for that process. Each row is a **page table entry (PTE)**, and it contains:

- The **physical frame number** (where in RAM this page lives)
- A **Present (P) bit**: 1 if the page is currently in RAM, 0 if swapped out or never allocated
- A **Dirty (D) bit**: 1 if the page has been written since it was loaded (and must be written back to disk before eviction)
- A **Accessed (A) bit**: 1 if the page was recently read or written (used by eviction algorithms)
- **Permission bits**: read, write, execute (enforced by the MMU on every access)
- A **User/Supervisor bit**: whether user-mode code can access this page

The OS switches the page table pointer (stored in a dedicated register — `CR3` on x86) every time it context-switches to a different process. From that moment, every virtual address the new process generates is translated using its own page table. Process isolation follows automatically.

Page tables also enable **copy-on-write (COW)**: when a process calls `fork()`, the OS does not copy all of the parent's RAM. Instead, it marks all pages in both processes as read-only and shares the physical frames. The first time either process tries to write a shared page, the MMU raises a protection fault, the OS copies just that one page, marks it writable, and resumes. This makes `fork()` nearly instant even for large processes.

sections.title: The TLB: Hardware Cache for Translations
sections.content:
If every memory access required a page-table lookup in RAM, performance would be disastrous — fetching a single byte would require two RAM accesses (one for the PTE, one for the byte itself). On a modern CPU doing billions of memory operations per second, that doubling overhead would halve performance at best.

The solution is the **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** — a small, extremely fast associative cache built into the MMU. It stores a small number of recently used virtual-page-to-physical-frame mappings (typically 32 to 1024 entries). On every memory access, the hardware checks the TLB first:

- **TLB hit**: the translation is found; the physical address is derived in 1–2 CPU cycles. The vast majority of real-world accesses are TLB hits because programs exhibit **spatial and temporal locality** — they tend to reuse the same pages repeatedly.
- **TLB miss**: the translation is not cached. The CPU (x86 uses hardware page-table walkers; MIPS and SPARC historically used software TLB handlers) walks the page table in RAM to find the PTE. This costs 10–100 cycles. The result is loaded into the TLB.
- **Page fault**: the PTE has its Present bit clear — the page is not in RAM. A hardware exception is raised, and the OS **page-fault handler** runs. It allocates a free frame, reads the page from disk (swap or a memory-mapped file), updates the PTE, and retries the instruction. Disk I/O means the cost is measured in *millions* of cycles.

The TLB is **flushed** (invalidated) on every context switch, because the next process's virtual addresses mean different things. Some architectures add **Address Space Identifiers (ASIDs)** to TLB entries, so entries from different processes can coexist — a significant optimization on systems that frequently context-switch.

**TLB reach** = number of TLB entries × page size. A 512-entry TLB covering 4 KB pages covers only 2 MB of memory. If your working set exceeds TLB reach, TLB misses become frequent — the cost of huge pages is that you use fewer TLB entries for the same footprint, dramatically reducing misses for large allocations.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  MA["Memory Access\n(virtual address)"] --> TLB{"TLB Lookup"}
  TLB -- "Hit (1-2 cycles)" --> PA["Physical Address\n→ access RAM"]
  TLB -- "Miss (10-100 cycles)" --> PTW["Hardware Page\nTable Walk"]
  PTW --> PTE{"PTE Present?"}
  PTE -- "Yes" --> LOAD["Load into TLB"]
  LOAD --> PA
  PTE -- "No" --> PF["Page Fault\n→ OS handler"]
  PF --> DISK["Load page\nfrom disk"]
  DISK --> LOAD
sections.caption: The three-tier address translation hierarchy: TLB hit is the fast path, a page-table walk handles TLB misses, and a page fault triggers the OS for pages not in RAM.

sections.title: Multi-Level Page Tables: Taming 64-Bit Address Spaces
sections.content:
A single-level (flat) page table for a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages needs 2³² / 2¹² = 2²⁰ = **one million entries**. At 4 bytes per entry that is 4 MB per process — manageable, though it adds up when you have hundreds of processes.

For a 64-bit address space the problem explodes: 2⁶⁴ / 2¹² = 2⁵² entries. At 8 bytes each, that is 36 petabytes per process for the flat table. Completely impractical.

The solution is a **multi-level page table** — a tree of tables where each level covers a fraction of the address bits. x86-64 Linux uses a **4-level** structure (5-level is also supported for very large address spaces):

1. **PGD** — Page Global Directory (bits 47–39): 512 entries pointing to PUDs
2. **PUD** — Page Upper Directory (bits 38–30): 512 entries pointing to PMDs
3. **PMD** — Page Middle Directory (bits 29–21): 512 entries pointing to PTs
4. **PT** — Page Table (bits 20–12): 512 entries, each a PTE with the frame number
5. **Offset** (bits 11–0): 4096 possible byte positions within the frame

The magic of multi-level tables: you only allocate intermediate-level nodes for regions of the address space that are actually in use. A typical 64-bit process uses only a tiny fraction of the 128 TB user-space address range. Code sits at low addresses; stack sits near the top; there is a vast unmapped gulf in between. The page table only needs entries for the occupied regions. A process with a 100 MB working set might need only a handful of PT-level pages instead of the astronomically large flat table.

The hardware page-table walker follows the chain on a TLB miss: load PGD from CR3, index into it to find the PUD address, load PUD, index into it to find PMD, and so on. Each level is another memory access — typically cached in L1/L2 since they are reused heavily.

flowchart TD

(PGD base addr)"] --> PGD["PGD
(512 entries)"]
  PGD --> PUD["PUD
(512 entries)"]
  PUD --> PMD["PMD
(512 entries)"]
  PMD --> PT["Page Table
(512 PTEs)"]

+ byte offset"]

47..39 | 38..30 | 29..21 | 20..12 | 11..0"] --> CR3

sections.title: Page Faults: Minor, Major, and Invalid
sections.content:
Not all page faults are equal. The OS page-fault handler distinguishes three cases:

**Minor (soft) page fault**: the page exists somewhere in physical RAM but is not yet mapped into this process's page table. This happens on first access after `malloc` (demand allocation), or when a process maps a shared library that another process already loaded. The handler only needs to update the PTE — no disk I/O. Cost: a few microseconds.

**Major (hard) page fault**: the page is genuinely not in RAM — it is in swap space or in a file on disk. The handler must:
1. Find a free physical frame (or evict a cold page to make room)
2. Schedule a disk read to load the page content
3. Block the faulting process until the read completes
4. Update the PTE and resume the process
Disk I/O makes this 1–10 *milliseconds* — about 1000× slower than a minor fault, and millions of times slower than a TLB hit.

**Invalid (segmentation fault)**: the virtual address is not mapped at all and is not a valid region (not in any VMA — virtual memory area). The OS sends SIGSEGV to the process. This is the crash your program gets when it dereferences a null pointer or writes past the end of an array — the hardware raises a page fault, the OS checks the page tables, finds no valid mapping, and kills the process.

Understanding the minor/major distinction is critical for performance analysis. Linux's `/proc/PID/status` shows `VmRSS` (physical resident pages), `VmSwap` (pages currently in swap), and `MinFlt`/`MajFlt` counters. A program accumulating major faults is hitting disk — a serious performance red flag.

sections.title: Swap Space and Page Eviction
sections.content:
When physical RAM fills up and a new page is needed, the OS must **evict** an existing page to make room. The eviction policy determines which page gets removed:

**LRU (Least Recently Used)**: evict the page that has not been accessed for the longest time. Pure LRU is expensive to implement in hardware for millions of pages, so real OSes use approximations.

**Clock algorithm (Linux: second-chance)**: pages are arranged in a circular list. A clock hand sweeps around; if a page's Accessed bit is set, the bit is cleared and the hand moves on (giving it a 'second chance'). If the bit is already clear when the hand reaches the page, that page is evicted. This approximates LRU with O(1) cost.

**Linux's multi-generational LRU (mglru)**: added in Linux 6.1, this groups pages into 'generations' based on recency. It tracks pages more accurately without the cost of pure LRU, significantly reducing thrashing on memory-pressured systems.

Evicted pages that have been modified (Dirty bit set) must be written to **swap space** (or a file) before their frame can be reused. Read-only pages (e.g., shared library code) can simply be discarded — the original file on disk serves as the backing store and can be re-read if needed.

**Thrashing** occurs when the system's **working set** — the set of pages actively needed by running processes — exceeds physical RAM. The OS evicts a page, another process immediately needs it back, so it evicts something else to bring it in, which displaces yet another needed page, and so on. CPU utilization collapses; the system spends nearly all its time on page I/O. Symptoms: `vmstat` shows consistently non-zero `si`/`so` (swap-in/swap-out) columns, high I/O wait, application latency spikes.

The **working set model** (introduced by Peter Denning in 1968) formalizes this: each process has a working set W(t, Δ) — the distinct pages it references in the time window Δ ending at t. If the sum of all processes' working sets exceeds RAM, thrashing is inevitable. The solution is to reduce the number of running processes until the total working set fits.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  RAM["Physical RAM\n(all frames full)"] --> EVICT["Choose victim page\n(LRU / Clock)"]
  EVICT --> DIRTY{"Page dirty?"}
  DIRTY -- "Yes" --> SWAP["Write to swap\nor file on disk"]
  DIRTY -- "No" --> FREE["Frame is free"]
  SWAP --> FREE
  FREE --> NEWPAGE["Load requested\npage into frame"]
  NEWPAGE --> PTE["Update PTE\n(Present=1)"]
sections.caption: Page eviction: when RAM is full, the OS picks a victim, writes it to disk if dirty, frees the frame, loads the requested page, and updates the page table.

sections.title: The Virtual Address Space Layout
sections.content:
On a 64-bit Linux system, each process's virtual address space is divided into regions called **VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas)**. The kernel maintains a red-black tree and linked list of VMAs per process. You can inspect them via `/proc/PID/maps`. The canonical layout from low to high addresses:

- **`0x0` (null page)**: unmapped deliberately, so null-pointer dereferences fault cleanly
- **Text segment** (`0x400000`): read-only, executable — compiled machine code of the program
- **Data segment**: initialized global variables (readable, writable, non-executable)
- **BSS segment**: uninitialized globals — the kernel zero-fills these pages on demand
- **Heap** (`brk`/`mmap`): grows upward; `malloc` expands it via the `sbrk` or `mmap` syscall
- **Memory-mapped region**: shared libraries, file-backed mappings, anonymous `mmap` allocations — placed by the kernel in the middle of the address space
- **Stack**: grows downward from near the top of user space; each thread gets its own stack; limited by `ulimit -s` (default 8 MB on Linux)
- **Kernel space** (`0xFFFF800000000000` and up on x86-64): mapped in every process's page table but marked Supervisor-only — user code cannot access it, but the kernel can access user memory without switching page tables

The separation of kernel space into every process's page table (marked inaccessible to user mode) is what makes system calls fast: the CPU can switch from user mode to kernel mode without changing `CR3` — no TLB flush needed. (The Meltdown vulnerability in 2017 broke this assumption and forced **KPTI** — Kernel Page Table Isolation — which uses separate page tables for user/kernel mode at the cost of a TLB flush on every syscall.)

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The BigInt literals (suffix `n`) let JavaScript handle 64-bit address arithmetic without loss of precision. The four 9-bit indices each select one of 512 entries in their respective page-table level; the 12-bit offset is the byte position within the 4 KB page. Nine bits × 4 levels + 12 offset bits = 48 usable virtual address bits on current x86-64 hardware.

sections.title: Memory-Mapped Files and Shared Memory
sections.content:
Virtual memory is not only for RAM — it is also the foundation of **memory-mapped I/O**. The `mmap` system call maps a file (or a device) directly into a process's virtual address space. Reading from that address range reads from the file; writing to it (with appropriate flags) writes back to the file via the OS page cache. The kernel manages the transfer of file blocks to and from physical RAM just like it manages swap pages.

This has several practical benefits:

- **Zero-copy I/O**: a process can read a large file at memory speed without explicit `read()` syscalls copying data through a kernel buffer. The OS loads file blocks on demand as pages.
- **Sharing between processes**: if two processes both `mmap` the same file, they share the same physical frames for its content. A write by one (with MAP_SHARED) is immediately visible to the other — the basis for inter-process shared memory without explicit IPC.
- **Executable loading**: the ELF loader (Linux) and Mach-O loader (macOS) do not copy the program binary into RAM at startup. They `mmap` the binary's segments. Code pages are loaded on demand as the program first executes them. Startup time is dramatically reduced for large programs.
- **The page cache**: Linux maintains a global **page cache** of file blocks in memory. When a process reads a file, the kernel places a copy in the page cache. Subsequent reads — by the same or a different process — are served from RAM. Memory-mapped files participate in the page cache directly.

The `MAP_ANONYMOUS` flag creates a memory-mapped region with no file backing — this is how `malloc` obtains large blocks from the kernel. It is also the mechanism behind shared anonymous mappings used for inter-process memory in `fork()`-based parallel programs.

sections.title: Copy-on-Write, fork, and Performance Implications
sections.content:
**Copy-on-write (COW)** is one of the most impactful applications of virtual memory. When a process calls `fork()`, the naive implementation would duplicate every byte of the parent's memory — gigabytes for a large server process. This would make `fork()` an expensive operation that degrades with process size.

With COW, the kernel instead:
1. Creates a new page table for the child process.
2. Copies the parent's page table entries into the child's, pointing both to the same physical frames.
3. Marks all shared pages **read-only** in both parent and child page tables.

The `fork()` returns almost instantly regardless of the process's working set. Physical memory is not copied at all yet. Now, when either process tries to write to a shared page, the MMU raises a protection fault (the page is read-only). The OS handler:
1. Allocates a new frame.
2. Copies the content of the original frame to the new one.
3. Updates the writing process's PTE to point to the new frame, with write permission.
4. Resumes execution.

Only the pages that are actually written are ever duplicated. If the child immediately calls `exec()` (as in a shell spawning a command), it replaces its address space entirely — no COW pages are ever copied. This is why the `fork()`+`exec()` idiom is efficient in Unix.

COW matters for application developers too. Redis uses `fork()` to create point-in-time snapshots (RDB persistence) without blocking writes: the child process iterates memory and writes to disk while the parent continues serving requests. Pages modified by the parent after the fork are COW-copied; pages not modified are shared. The total extra memory used equals the **write amplification** during the snapshot window.

A common gotcha: if you pre-allocate a large data structure, then `fork()`, and the parent immediately begins modifying it, the COW copies can push memory usage significantly — sometimes causing OOM (Out of Memory) kills. Tools like `smem` report **PSS** (Proportional Set Size), which divides shared pages proportionally among sharing processes, giving a more accurate picture than RSS.

sequenceDiagram
  participant Parent
  participant OS
  participant Child
  Parent->>OS: fork()
  OS->>OS: Copy page tables, mark all pages read-only
  OS->>Child: return 0 (child)
  OS->>Parent: return child_pid (parent)
  Parent->>OS: Write to page 0x1000 (COW fault)
  OS->>OS: Allocate new frame, copy page content
  OS->>Parent: Resume with private writable copy
  Child->>OS: Read page 0x1000
  OS->>Child: Serve from original shared frame
sections.caption: Copy-on-Write during fork: pages are shared read-only until a write triggers a fault, at which point only the written page is physically duplicated.

sections.content: **Historical context:** Virtual memory was not invented with the modern OS in mind. The **Atlas computer** at Manchester University (1962) introduced paging and demand paging — the first machine to automatically move programs between drum storage and core memory. IBM's **OS/360** introduced segmentation. The VAX/VMS operating system (1977) refined the multi-level page table approach that x86 later adopted. The concept of the **working set** was formalized by Peter Denning in his 1968 paper, which remains foundational reading for OS designers. Modern Linux's memory management — with its multi-generational LRU, huge pages, NUMA awareness, and memory cgroups — is the direct descendant of those 1960s ideas, scaled to machines with terabytes of RAM and hundreds of CPU cores.

**Common mistakes and interview insights:**
- **Confusing virtual size and RSS**: `top` shows both VIRT and RES. VIRT can be enormous (hundreds of GB for JVM processes) because it includes reserved-but-not-touched regions. RSS is the physically resident subset — the number that actually matters for memory pressure.
- **Forgetting that fork duplicates page tables, not pages**: COW means `fork()` is O(n) in page-table entries, not O(n) in working set size. But subsequent writes do cost physical RAM.
- **Null is address zero**: most languages trap null-pointer dereferences because the OS deliberately leaves the first page (often the first 64 KB) unmapped. Accessing address 0 raises a page fault with no valid mapping → SIGSEGV.
- **Meltdown/Spectre**: these CPU vulnerabilities exploited speculative execution to read kernel memory from user mode by abusing TLB and cache state — a reminder that virtual memory isolation is implemented in hardware and hardware bugs can break it.
- **Stack overflow is literally that**: when a thread's stack grows downward past its allocated VMA, the next page has no mapping → page fault → SIGSEGV. Guard pages (unmapped pages just below the stack VMA) catch this reliably.

items: **Virtual memory** gives every process a private, isolated address space. The OS+MMU silently translate every virtual address to a physical RAM address, preventing processes from accessing each other's memory.

Memory is divided into fixed-size **pages** (typically 4 KB). A virtual address splits into a page number (translated by the page table) and a byte offset (passed through unchanged). Page tables store one entry per virtual page, not per byte.

The **TLB** is a hardware cache of recent translations. A TLB hit costs ~1–2 cycles; a TLB miss triggers a page-table walk (10–100 cycles); a **page fault** may cost a disk I/O (millions of cycles). Locality is critical to TLB efficiency.

**Multi-level page tables** (4-level on x86-64) avoid allocating storage for the astronomically large flat tables a 64-bit space would require, by only creating intermediate nodes for address ranges actually in use.

**Demand paging** allocates physical frames lazily — `malloc` reserves virtual space instantly; physical RAM is only consumed when a page is first accessed (triggering a minor page fault). RSS tracks actual physical usage.

**Copy-on-write** makes `fork()` nearly instant: parent and child share physical frames read-only until a write triggers a per-page copy. Redis uses this for snapshot persistence; shells use it for command execution.

**Thrashing** occurs when the total working set of running processes exceeds physical RAM. The OS spends more time evicting and reloading pages than executing code. The cure is reducing concurrent processes, adding RAM, or using huge pages to reduce TLB pressure.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of the Memory Management Unit (MMU)?
options: To schedule which process runs on the CPU next
To translate virtual addresses to physical addresses on every memory access
To compress data stored in RAM to save space
To manage the disk read/write queue
quiz.explanation: The MMU is a hardware unit inside the CPU that intercepts every memory access and translates the virtual address the process uses into the physical address where the data actually lives in RAM, using the TLB and page tables.

quiz.question: A virtual address on a system with 4 KB pages splits into which two components?
options: Segment number and segment offset
Process ID and byte index
Page number (upper bits) and byte offset within the page (lower 12 bits)
Frame number and TLB index
quiz.explanation: For 4 KB (2^12) pages, the lower 12 bits are the byte offset within the page and pass through the MMU unchanged. The upper bits are the virtual page number, which is looked up in the page table to find the physical frame number.

quiz.question: Which page fault type requires disk I/O and is the most expensive?
options: Minor (soft) fault — page in RAM but not yet mapped to this process
Major (hard) fault — page not in RAM, must be loaded from swap or file
Invalid fault — null pointer dereference causing SIGSEGV
TLB fault — translation not cached in the TLB
quiz.explanation: A major (hard) page fault means the page is not currently in physical RAM at all. The OS must read it from swap space or a file on disk, which takes 1–10 milliseconds — about 1000× slower than a minor fault and millions of times slower than a TLB hit.

quiz.question: Why do 64-bit systems use multi-level page tables instead of a single flat table?
options: Multi-level tables enable faster TLB lookups
A flat table for 2^64 addresses would require petabytes of memory per process
Single-level tables cannot store permission bits
Hardware MMUs only support walking four levels, not one
quiz.explanation: A flat page table for a 64-bit address space (2^52 possible 4 KB pages) would need approximately 36 petabytes per process. Multi-level tables only allocate intermediate nodes for address regions that are actually in use, making the table proportional to the working set, not the total address space.

quiz.question: What does Copy-on-Write (COW) accomplish during a fork() call?
options: It immediately copies all of the parent's physical pages into new frames for the child
It shares physical frames between parent and child as read-only; a write triggers per-page duplication
It prevents the child from writing any memory until exec() is called
It copies only the stack pages; heap pages are always shared
quiz.explanation: COW marks all pages shared read-only in both parent and child page tables. Only when a process actually writes to a page does the MMU raise a protection fault, at which point the OS copies just that one page to a new frame. This makes fork() nearly instant regardless of process size.

quiz.question: What is 'thrashing' and what does it indicate?
options: Rapid CPU context-switching overhead between many threads
A condition where the OS spends more time swapping pages than executing processes because the working set exceeds RAM
Memory fragmentation that prevents large contiguous allocations
TLB invalidation storms caused by too many concurrent processes
quiz.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the combined working set of running processes exceeds physical RAM. The OS constantly evicts pages that are immediately needed again, resulting in near-continuous disk I/O and collapsing CPU utilization. Adding RAM or reducing the number of concurrent processes resolves it.

quiz.question: When a process calls malloc() for 1 GB on a system with 512 MB free RAM, what typically happens immediately?
options: malloc() returns NULL because insufficient physical RAM is available
The OS immediately allocates 1 GB from swap space
Virtual address space is reserved but physical frames are only allocated on first access (demand paging)
The OS begins evicting other processes to free 1 GB of RAM synchronously
quiz.explanation: Modern OSes use optimistic (lazy) allocation. malloc() reserves virtual address space and returns a pointer immediately. Physical frames are only committed when the process first touches each page (a minor page fault). This is why a process's virtual size can far exceed its RSS.

quiz.question: What does the TLB's 'reach' represent, and why does it matter for performance?
options: The maximum number of processes whose page tables can be cached simultaneously
The total physical memory addressable without a TLB miss, equal to TLB entries times page size
The number of CPU cycles saved per TLB hit compared to a full page-table walk
The distance in bytes between two consecutive TLB entries
quiz.explanation: TLB reach = number of TLB entries × page size. A 512-entry TLB with 4 KB pages covers only 2 MB. If a process's working set exceeds TLB reach, misses become frequent and expensive. Huge pages (2 MB) dramatically increase reach, reducing TLB miss rates for large workloads like databases.

quiz.question: What is the Dirty bit in a page table entry used for?
options: To mark pages that contain invalid or corrupted data
To indicate that a page has been written since it was loaded, meaning it must be saved to disk before eviction
To flag pages that belong to the kernel and are inaccessible to user processes
To record the number of times a page has been accessed for LRU eviction
quiz.explanation: The Dirty bit is set by the MMU when a process writes to a page. During eviction, only dirty pages need to be written to swap or a backing file — clean pages (like read-only code) can simply be discarded and re-read from their original source if needed later.

quiz.question: Why does the Linux kernel map its own address space into every process's page table, marked as Supervisor-only?
options: So the kernel can execute system calls without switching to a separate kernel process
To allow user processes to read kernel data structures directly for performance
Because the kernel occupies the lower half of the 64-bit address space
To enable the kernel to evict process pages without changing CR3
quiz.explanation: Mapping kernel space into every process's page table (but marking it Supervisor-only) means a system call can transition from user mode to kernel mode without changing CR3 — avoiding a TLB flush. Only the CPU privilege level changes. The Meltdown vulnerability broke this by leaking kernel data via speculative execution, prompting KPTI which switched to separate page tables at the cost of TLB flushes on every syscall.
